background.definition: Stasis dermatitis is a chronic skin condition caused by chronic venous insufficiency (CVI). The increased venous pressure leads to hyperpigmentation of the skin, pruritus, weeping, erosions, and crusting. Venous leg ulcers (VLUs) are wounds that occur on the lower legs of patients with venous insufficiency disease.

list.listitem: Accurate estimates for the prevalence of VLUs in different countries are lacking.
In the U.S., the prevalence of leg ulcers among adults ranges from 1% to 2%. VLUs account for about 70% of cases, whereas arterial ulcers or mixed arterio-venous ulcers make up around 20% of cases.
In 2011, the point prevalence of VLUs in Leeds, U.K. (population >750,000) was 2.9 per 10,000.
A 2014 study in the U.S. estimated the total cost of treating VLUs at nearly $15 billion annually.
Another U.S. study from 2014 estimated the mean total cost of treating one VLU in the outpatient setting to be $10,851, and $33,629 if treatment necessitates hospitalization.
Chronic venous insufficiency (CVI) characterized by chronic venous hypertension as a result of valvular dysfunction or venous obstruction

CVI is caused by venous valvular dysfunction, obstruction of venous flow, inadequate venous return due to poor calf muscle pump function, or a combination of these processes. Rarely, congenital venous anomalies contribute to this condition.

Postthrombotic syndrome (PTS) or postphlebitic syndrome occurs as a sequelae of deep venous thrombosis (DVT). The thrombus obstructs venous flow and leads to chronic venous hypertension and the characteristic changes of CVI.

Red blood cells extravasate out of the capillary system because of the increased venous pressure and then break down in the dermis. This leads to the characteristic hyperpigmentation of stasis dermatitis.
The dermatitis usually progresses to skin fibrosis (dermatosclerosis) and avascular areas that are prone to excoriation, ulceration, and poor healing.
To prevent VLU recurrence, recommend the use of compression stockings of at least 20 mm Hg pressure at the ankles. Higher compression may be more effective at the cost of lower compliance. A
High-quality evidence is lacking for the use of compression stockings as primary prevention for patients with varicose veins or chronic venous insufficiency without prior ulceration. A
Evidence is lacking for the use of compression stockings to prevent CVI among workers who stand for long periods of time (e.g., flight attendants). B

Compared to no intervention or placebo stockings, use of elastic compression stockings of at least 20 mm Hg may decrease the incidence of PTS among patients with a history of DVT, based on low-quality evidence. B
Inadequate anticoagulation (INR <2.0 over 50% of the time) during treatment for acute DVT for three months increases the risk of PTS. B
Consider a diagnosis of VLU in patients presenting with superficial, irregular, exudative ulcer of the gaiter area, with associated leg edema, varicosities and venous stasis changes. C
Obtain ankle-brachial index (ABI) in patients presenting with likely VLU to evaluate for concomitant PAD. C

In patients with VLU present for 6 weeks to 6 months, consider early evaluation for superficial venous reflux using venous duplex ultrasonography as these patients may benefit from early endovenous ablation. A

list.listitem: Signs of venous stasis include hemosiderin staining or hyperpigmentation, xerosis (dryness), varicosities, leg edema, lipodermatosclerosis ("inverted champagne bottle" leg appearance), and atrophie blanche (characterized by porcelain white scars, dyspigmentation and telangiectasias).

VLUs are usually located on the gaiter area, referring to the area of the lower leg near the medial malleolus up to the mid-calf. They are usually painful, shallow, with irregular but defined borders, moderate to heavy exudate, and often have necrotic tissue or slough.

During the history, inquire about risk factors for chronic venous disease: history of DVT or pulmonary embolism, previous leg injuries, sedentary lifestyle, or family history of venous disease. Risk factors for first VLU include history of nonvenous leg ulcer, male gender, chronic venous hypertension, and older age.

To assess for risk of nonvenous (i.e., arterial or neuropathic) disease, ask about smoking history, claudication, history of coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease.

Two criteria have been proposed for the clinical assessment of wounds with bacterial colonization (NERDS) or infection (STONEES). NERDS stands for Nonhealing (no size change in 2-4 weeks), Exudate increase, Red friable granulation tissue, Debris or necrotic tissue, and Smell. STONEES evaluate for Size enlargement, Temperature increase, Os (bone exposure or probing), New areas of breakdown, Exudate increase, Erythema or Edema, and Smell.

Obtain ankle-brachial index (ABI) in patients presenting with likely VLU to evaluate for coexisting PAD. ABI of less than 0.8 is suggestive of PAD, whereas patients with ABI of 0.5 or less should be referred to a vascular surgeon for evaluation for revascularization or clearance for compression therapy.

In patients with VLU present for 6 weeks to 6 months, consider early evaluation for superficial venous reflux using venous duplex ultrasonography as these patients may benefit from early venous ablation.

Consider performing tissue biopsy and/or culture in patients who are not responding to empiric treatment of wound infection to investigate other causes of leg ulcers (e.g., atypical infection, malignancy, vasculitis, inflammatory dermatoses, etc.).

A Clinical decision rule was developed in 260 patients and validated in 219 patients with venous leg ulcer at a dermatology clinic. Patients with VLU <5 cm2 for <6 months had a 95% healing rate with Unna Boot use. Those with VLU >5 cm2 for >6 months had a healing rate between 13% and 37%. Those with only one risk factor had a 73% healing rate.

The VLU Wound Healing Index (VLU WHI), a risk stratification tool for clinical and research use, was developed based on inclusion of over 11,000 VLUs to assist in early identification of wounds that may be difficult to heal. The findings, which were then validated using a 10% validation sample, identified the following VLU predictors of difficulty healing: larger number of concurrent wounds from any source, increasing wound size, increasing age of wound, presence of bioburden or infection, being non-ambulatory, and being hospitalized.
See - Algorithm for the evaluation of patients with venous leg ulcer
The initial step in the evaluation and management of patients with VLUs is determining the ABI of each affected leg. If ABI is 0.8 or greater, compression therapy can be safely started.

If ABI is below 0.8, patient needs to be referred to vascular surgery for evaluation for revascularization or for clearance for compression therapy. In general, legs with ABI between 0.5 to 0.8 can undergo light (<20 mm Hg) to moderate (20-30 mm Hg) compression under close supervision of a trained wound care specialist. If ABI is below 0.5 or ankle pressure below 60 mmHg, compression should not be started until thorough vascular consultation has been accomplished.
Pentoxifylline in combination with compression therapy is effective in treating VLUs. It may also be effective without compression therapy. A

Compression therapy using multi-component bandages, systems with elastic component, and high-compression systems (30-40 mmHg pressure at the ankles) improves VLU healing rates. Compression therapy also improves pain and disease-specific quality of life. A
Early endovenous ablation, when added to compression therapy, speeds ulcer healing and prolongs ulcer-free time among patients with superficial venous reflux. A
Uncomplicated stasis dermatitis may respond to short-term topical corticosteroid treatment. B

Pentoxifylline is a drug that improves blood flow and decreases thrombosis. Alone or in combination with compression therapy, pentoxifylline improves healing rates of VLUs more than placebo (or no treatment) or placebo with compression, respectively. The most common side effect is gastrointestinal disturbance and can be mitigated by taking the medication with meals and slow titration of the dose over three weeks (to a target dose of 1200 mg/day, in 3 divided doses).

Studies have had mixed results regarding the use of aspirin to treat VLUs. One concluded that enteric-coated aspirin (at least 300 mg daily) improves healing of VLU when added to standard compression therapy. However, a more recent double-blind study with 251 adults with open leg ulcer for at least 4 weeks found no benefit (time to healing 77 days with aspirin, 69 days with placebo, p = 0.25). In 2016, a Cochrane review concluded, based on low-quality evidence from 2 RCTs, that the current evidence is not sufficient to make definitive recommendations for the use of aspirin in treating VLUs.

Systemic antibiotic therapy should be reserved for VLU infection, and choice of agent should be based on culture and sensitivities if possible. A Cochrane review in 2014 concluded that there is no evidence that systemic antibiotics improves healing of noninfected VLUs.

Statins have vasoactive and anti-inflammatory properties. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-center study of 66 patients found simvastatin 40mg daily plus compression to be better than placebo plus compression in patients with VLUs present for at least 3 months and smaller than 10 cm in diameter. The primary outcome of complete ulcer healing at 10 weeks was more common in simvastatin group (90% vs 34%; p <0.05; NNT = 2). For subgroup of small ulcers (<5 cm diameter), 100% ulcers healed compared with 50% in placebo group. The time to healing among the simvastatin group was faster for small ulcers (6.9 vs 8.4 weeks; p <0.001).

Sulodexide is a highly purified glycosaminoglycan predominantly made up of heparin and has profibrinolytic, antithrombotic, and antiinflammatory properties. It is administered orally or intravenously and has mainly been studied in thrombotic diseases. A Cochrane review found low-quality evidence that sulodexide, added to local wound care and compression, improves VLU healing.
Oral zinc does not appear to be effective in promoting VLU healing, based on 6 trials with 183 participants (RR 1.2; 95% CI 0.9-1.7).

In a small study with methodological shortcomings, intravenous iloprost, an anti-inflammatory drug, at a dose of 0.5 to 2 ng/kg/min 6 hours per day, 5 days a week for 3 weeks, was associated with a higher rate of more rapid and complete healing (100% vs 85%).
Application of Eutectic Mixture of Local Anesthetics (EMLA) 5% cream over VLU appears to decrease pain during debridement.

A Cochrane review found no RCTs comparing cleansing versus no cleansing to treat VLUs. Additionally, it found uncertainty regarding the effectiveness of various wound cleansers, including sterile water, saline, Ringer's solution, polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB), aqueous oxygen peroxide, propyl betaine, polihexanide, and octenidine dihydrochloride/phenoxyethanol (OHP). All included RCTs had significant methodological shortcomings, hence more rigorous trials are needed.

Antiseptics and topical antibiotics should be used judiciously for mild wound infections. A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for their effectiveness in treating VLUs compared to nonmedicated dressings. However, 4 RCTs involving 72 patients appear to show, based on low-certainty evidence, that hydrogen peroxide may heal VLUs faster than standard care in the short-term.

A small RCT involving 43 participants found timolol gel 0.5% applied every 2 days over 12 weeks, when added to standard care (interface dressings plus compression), was superior to standard care alone in reducing VLUs by 40% at 12 weeks (67% vs. 32%). No serious adverse events were noted in the study; however 5 local wound infections (not requiring systemic antibiotics) occurred with topical timolol vs 1 local infection in the control group. The authors recommend larger multicenter trials be conducted before routinely recommending topical timolol to treat VLUs.
Evidence regarding the use of growth factors such as platelet-rich plasma and epidermal growth factor for treating VLU is uncertain.
In a double-blind RCT of 19 patients, topical betamethasone valerate 0.12% foam applied twice daily appears to be safe and likely provides short-term improvement of venous stasis dermatitis.

The effectiveness of surgical debridement to facilitate VLU healing is not known, based on a 2015 Cochrane review that found no RCTs on the subject. Evidence from a large retrospective study of 312,744 wounds of any cause suggests that higher frequency of debridement of any type (ie, surgical and nonsurgical), compared to lower frequency of debridement, appears to heal wounds faster and results to more wounds healed.
Skin grafting using a bilayer human skin equivalent plus compression therapy heals VLUs faster than standard dressings plus compression, based on a Cochrane review.

A multicenter trial in the United Kingdom randomized 450 VLU patients to early endovenous ablation (within 2 weeks) plus compression versus compression plus delayed ablation (after ulcer has healed or after 6 months if ulcer has not healed). The median time to healing was faster with early ablation (56 vs 82 days), the likelihood of healing at 24 weeks was greater (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.1 to 1.7), and patients had longer ulcer-free time at 12 months. A Cochrane review evaluating 2 RCTs involving 506 patients (450 of whom are from above UK study) concluded that superficial endovenous ablation plus compression therapy improves VLU healing compared to compression alone, based on high-certainty evidence. Based on European standards, this approach appears to be cost-effective for VLU patients at 1 year.
A 2019 Cochrane review found uncertainty in the role of subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery for the treatment of VLUs, considering the low- to very low-certainty evidence of the 4 included RCTs.
Horse chestnut seed 300 mg (standardized to 50 mg of escin, the active ingredient) twice daily may provide symptom relief for patients with chronic venous insufficiency.
Honey as a treatment for VLU has unclear benefits, based on a Cochrane review that evaluated 2 trials with 476 patients. Evidence was deemed low quality.
Efficacy of topical Aloe vera for the treatment of acute and chronic wounds is uncertain, based on a Cochrane review of 7 studies involving 347 participants.

A Cochrane review on phlebotonics for treating CVI found moderate-certainty evidence that phlebotonics may slightly decrease leg edema, moderate-certainty evidence that it does not improve quality of life, low-certainty evidence that it does not improve VLU healing, and moderate-certainty evidence that it causes more side effects compared to placebo. Phlebotonics are substances that occur naturally or are synthesized that enhance marcocirculation (ie, venoactive) and microcirculation.

A Cochrane review found low-quality evidence that flavonoids hasten VLU healing, but the highest-quality study did not find flavonoids effective. Flavoinoids occur naturally in tea, chocolate, cocoa, and red wine, but controlled trials have used purified oral forms.

Compression therapy appears to heal more VLUs and shorten healing time than no compression, based on two Cochrane reviews. Multi-component bandages appear more effective than single-component bandages; those with elastic components are better than those without. Furthermore, four-layer bandages or high-compression systems (30-40 mmHg) are more effective than short-stretch or inelastic bandages (e.g., Unna boot, Coban). Compression therapy also improves pain and disease-specific quality of life. Two-layer hoses and four-layer bandages that deliver high compression (at least 40 mmHg) appear similarly effective in treating VLUs.

Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) is better than no compression for VLU healing, but it is uncertain if it can replace compression bandages as primary treatment. Limited evidence suggests that compression bandages plus IPC is better than compression bandages alone, and that rapid IPC is more effective than slow IPC.

Based on a Cochrane review of 3 RCTs, there is insufficient evidence for the effectiveness of interventions to help patients adhere to compression therapy. These interventions include community-based programs using home-based care, nurse-led self management programs, and video or paper handout patient education materials.
A randomized trial (n = 84) found that adding compression therapy to patient education reduced the likelihood of recurrent cellulitis in patients with chronic leg edema (NNT = 4).

Dressings should maintain a moist wound environment and keep the periwound dry. Despite the wide availability of wet-to-dry dressings, they should be avoided since they cause more pain, prolong nursing time, and lead to lower patient satisfaction.

VLUs are generaly wet, exudative wounds. Use of absorbent dressings such as alginate or foarm dressings is generally recommended. Two Cochrane reviews concluded that there is insufficient evidence for the efficacy of alginate or foam dressings over other dressings such as nonadherent or hydrocolloid dressings for the treatment of VLUs. However, the reviewers acknowledged other important considerations for using absorbent dressings, including patient preference, exudate management, and potential cost savings from less frequent dressing changes.

In 2018, Cochrane released a network meta-analysis of dressings and topical agents for the treatment of VLUs and concluded that additional studies are necessary to identify effective therapies, considering the whole network and individual comparisons had low certainty.
Ibuprofen slow-release foam dressings may provide short-term pain relief for VLU patients with persistent wound pain.

Low-certainty evidence from a Cochrane review suggests that hydrogel may be more effective than parrafin gauze in performing autolytic debridement of VLUs. However, a later Cochrane review found inconclusive evidence for hydrogel dressings compared to saline gauze, alginate, manuka honey, or hydrocolloid dressings for improving VLU healing.

The efficacy of protease-modulating matrix (PMM) dressings for VLU is uncertain, based on low-quality evidence. Testing the wound exudate for elevated protease activity then using PMM dressings only for VLUs with elevated protease activity has been proposed as an efficacious and cost-effective strategy. However, a Cochrane review found no RCTs to evaluate this "test and treat" method.

Compared to neutral vehicle, hyaluronic acid-containing dressings and topical agents may improve VLU healing (moderate-certainty) and pain (low-certainty), based on a Cochrane review of 12 RCTs involving 1108 patients.
Two systematic reviews failed to show the efficacy of negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) for VLUs.
The effectiveness of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT), therapeutic ultrasound, electromagnetic therapy, and extracorporeal shock wave therapy for treating VLUs is uncertain.
Progressive resistance exercise plus physical activity, in combination with compression therapy, appear to hasten VLU healing, based on a systematic review of 6 studies with 230 patients.

For individuals with chronic venous insufficiency without ulcers, it is unclear whether physical exercise improves pain and quality of life, based on a Cochrane review of 5 RCTs involving 146 individuals.

Balneotherapy refers to therapies involving water, including immersing in natural mineral or thermal waters. A Cochrane review of 9 RCTs involving 1126 patients with CVI found moderate-certainty evidence that balneotherapy improves disease severity signs and symptoms as measured by the Venous Clinical Severity Score (VCSS), and low-certainty evidence that it may improve pain and skin pigmentation. However, balneotherapy does not appear more effective than no treatment in improving leg edema or the incidence of VLUs.

Since nutritional status may influence wound healing, patients with chronic, nonhealing ulcers or with suspected nutritional deficiencies should be evaluated using validated nutritional assessment tools (e.g., Subjective Global Assessment [SGA], Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool [MUST], Mini Nutritional Assessment [MNA]), or referred to a registered dietitian.
A leg ulcer care pathway may significantly accelerate VLU healing time at 12 months compared to usual care (80% vs 20%, P < 0.001), based on a prospective cohort study in the UK.

A community nursing intervention, the Lindsay Leg Club model of care emphasizing socialization and peer support, was found to be more effective than a traditional community nursing model in improved quality of life, morale, self-esteem, healing, pain, and functional ability for patients with chronic VLUs.

Efficacy of autolytic debridement to treat VLUs is supported by limited evidence, based on a Cochrane review. While studies were of low quality and findings mixed, some dressings and topical agents that may possess effective autolytic properties include hydrogel, dextranomer, biocellulose, honey, cadexomer iodine, and hydrocolloid dressings.

Biologic debridement, which utilizes medical larvae or maggots, is not supported by moderate- or high-certainty evidence as a safe, efficacious, and cost-effective treatment for VLUs, based on a Cochrane review.

Despite the wide availability of wet-to-dry dressings as a form of mechanical debridement, they should be avoided since they cause more pain, prolong nursing time, and lead to lower patient satisfaction.

With adequate treatment, most VLUs should show a decrease in size after 3 months of treatment and healing after 12 months of treatment. Failure of an ulcer to improve should prompt a referral or further investigation (i.e., tissue biopsy or culture).

Refer VLU patients with coexisting arterial insufficiency to vascular surgery, espcially if ABI is less than 0.8. In addition, VLU patients with superficial venous reflux should be referred to vascular surgery for evaluation for early endovenous ablation.

Refer patient to a wound care specialist if VLU has not improved in 4 weeks despite adequate treatment, for evaluation of atypical causes of leg ulcer, surgical tissue coverage (e.g., grafting), advanced compression therapy, specialized dressings, and other adjunctive therapies.
Hospitalize VLU patients presenting with systemic symptoms, especially those with severe comorbidities like poorly-controlled diabetes, immunocompromised status, or rapidly worsening wound infection.
Patients with venous ulcer <5 cm2 for less than six months have a 95% healing rate with Unna Boot use. B
Predictors of VLU healing include superficial venous ablation and percentage of wound reduction after 4 weeks of treatment, based on a prospective study of 104 patients with large, chronic VLUs. B
It is unclear whether elevated protease activity, measured as a biomarker from exudate of chronic wounds, is associated with prolonged VLU healing time. B
A leg ulcer care pathway may significantly accelerate VLU healing time at 12 months compared to usual care (80% vs 20%, P < 0.001), based on a prospective cohort study in the UK. B
